options.text: the energy transferred per unit charge
options.explanation: That is the definition of voltage, not current.

options.text: how fast electric charge streams past a point
options.explanation: Current counts how much charge passes each second.

options.text: the force pushing electrons through a wire
options.explanation: No force appears anywhere in the definition of current.

options.text: the number of electrons sitting inside a wire
options.explanation: Owning electrons is not the same as moving them; current needs flow.

options.text: one joule of energy carried by one coulomb
options.explanation: A joule per coulomb defines a volt.

options.text: one volt across one ohm of resistance
options.explanation: That combination belongs to the voltage-current-resistance equation, not the ampere.

options.text: one watt delivered for one second
options.explanation: A watt times a second is a joule of energy, not a flow of charge.

options.text: one coulomb of charge flowing past each second
options.explanation: One amp means one coulomb arriving every second.

options.text: in series with the component being measured
options.explanation: The meter must feel the same current as the component, so it sits in the same path.
That is the voltmeter's placement; an ammeter in parallel misreads the circuit.
Placement matters: only in series does it read the component's current.
Placing it across the cell measures the cell, not the component in question.

questions.stem: Conventional current is taken to flow:

options.text: negative terminal back to the positive one
options.explanation: That is the direction of electron flow, not conventional current.

options.text: in the same direction as the electrons move
options.explanation: Electrons are negative, so they drift against the conventional arrow.

options.text: positive terminal out to the negative one
options.explanation: The convention sends current out of the positive terminal and back into the negative one.
Current travels the whole loop, wires included.

questions.stem: A charge of 6 C flows past a point in a circuit in 2 s. The current is:

options.explanation: That multiplies charge by time instead of dividing.
That divides time by charge, flipping the ratio.
Current = charge ÷ time = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 A.
Adding the two quantities is meaningless here.

questions.stem: State what electric current measures and give its unit.
questions.modelAnswer: Current measures the rate at which electric charge flows through a component, and it is measured in amperes (A).

questions.stem: How should an ammeter be connected when measuring the current through a lamp?
questions.modelAnswer: In series with the lamp, so the same current that passes through the lamp also passes through the meter.

questions.stem: Explain why scientists describe current as flowing from positive to negative even though electrons move the other way.
questions.modelAnswer: The positive-to-negative direction was chosen as the convention before electrons were discovered, and scientists kept it after the electron turned out to drift the opposite way.

questions.stem: A charge of 15 C flows through a torch bulb in 60 s. Calculate the current.
questions.modelAnswer: Current = charge ÷ time = 15 C ÷ 60 s = 0.25 A.

questions.stem: In a metal wire, the charge carriers that make up the current are:

options.text: positive ions fixed in the metal lattice
options.explanation: Lattice ions vibrate in place; they do not drift along the wire.

options.text: free electrons, which carry negative charge
options.explanation: Metal conductors conduct through their negatively charged electrons.
Nuclear protons never roam a circuit wire.

options.text: whole atoms drifting along the wire
options.explanation: Atoms stay in the lattice; only their loose electrons travel.

questions.stem: The equation linking charge, current and time is:

options.explanation: Dividing by time gives the current, not the charge.
Charge accumulates at the rate I for a duration t.
That inverts the rate relationship.
Different units cannot simply be added.

questions.stem: How much charge flows when a current of 4 A runs for 10 s?

options.explanation: That divides time by current instead of multiplying.
Adding current and time is meaningless.
That divides current by time, giving the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Electrons drift through a cell from:

options.text: positive to negative, like conventional current
options.explanation: Electrons are negative, so they move against the conventional arrow.

options.text: negative to positive, opposite to conventional current
options.explanation: Negative carriers drift the opposite way to the conventional direction.
The drift has one net direction around the loop.

options.text: nowhere — electrons stay fixed in the metal
options.explanation: Fixed electrons could never carry a current.

questions.stem: A current quoted as 10 mA expressed in amperes is:

options.explanation: That scales the wrong way: milli means one thousandth.
That ignores the milli prefix entirely.
That treats milli as one tenth.

questions.stem: Write down the equation linking charge, current and time, stating the unit of each quantity.
questions.modelAnswer: Q = I × t, with charge Q in coulombs (C), current I in amperes (A) and time t in seconds (s).

questions.stem: What carries the current inside a metal wire?
questions.modelAnswer: A flow of negatively charged electrons drifts through the metal when a voltage drives them.

questions.stem: Explain why conventional current and electron flow point in opposite directions.
questions.modelAnswer: Conventional current was fixed as the direction positive charge would move, before anyone knew electrons existed; once electrons were found to be negative carriers, their drift turned out to run the other way, but the convention was kept.

questions.stem: A motor draws a current of 0.5 A for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows through it.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert first: 2 minutes = 120 s. Then Q = I × t = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C.
